title: Renovating? Put a Scrap Metal Bin on Site
description: A renovation turns up more metal than you'd expect. In a skip you pay to get rid of it; in a scrap bin we pay you for it. Here's how to make it work.

body.text: A renovation turns up more metal than most people expect: old roofing iron, guttering, copper pipe, a hot water system, the laundry tub. Put it in a skip with the rubbish and you pay to get rid of it. Put it in a scrap metal bin and we pay you for it.

Book the bin before the work starts. Tell us what you're pulling out, roughly how much and where the bin should go, and we'll suggest a size. We have bins in different sizes, but most jobs end up with a 1 m³ or a 2.4 m³ bin. Throwing metal straight into a bin is far easier than moving a pile of it twice.

Pick the spot. The bin needs firm, level ground with room for our truck to get in and out. If it has to go on the road or the nature strip, you'll usually need a permit from your council, so check with them before you book.

Keep it to metal. Steel, iron, copper, brass and aluminium can all go in, along with roofing, fencing, guttering, old tools and washing machines or stoves. Rubbish, timber, plastic and green waste can't, and neither can gas bottles, aerosol cans, drums with fuel or oil in them, fridges or air conditioners that still hold gas, or anything with asbestos in it.

Set the good stuff aside. Copper pipe, brass taps and aluminium window frames are worth far more than steel, and clean, sorted metal gets a better price than a mixed load. Keep them in a bucket on the side and bring them in yourself, or ask us about keeping them separate in the bin.

Call us when it's full. We'll collect it, or swap it for an empty one if the job isn't finished, then weigh it at our Hallam yard and pay you for the metal by bank transfer the same day. Have your photo ID and your BSB and account number handy.

title: Getting the Best Price for Scrap Aluminium
description: Window frames, sheet, castings and cans each have their own price. How to spot aluminium, strip it and sort it so you're paid the most for every kilo.

body.text: Aluminium turns up everywhere: old window frames, pergolas, ladders, boat parts, lawn mower decks and the cans from a summer of barbecues. It's light, so it doesn't look like much on the trailer, but every kilo is worth far more than steel.

Make sure it's aluminium. It's light, silver-grey and a magnet won't stick to it. Stainless steel looks similar and a magnet won't stick to most of it either, but it's much heavier for its size. Aluminium weighs about a third as much as steel.

Know the grades. Clean extrusion, such as window and door frames, pays best. Sheet, plate and old signs are graded on their own, and so are castings like engine heads and gearbox housings. Alloy wheels are a high grade of their own once the tyres, weights and valve stems are off.

Strip the frames. Window frames with the glass, rubber seals, flyscreen mesh and steel screws removed are paid at the clean price. Left on, they pull the grade down, and broken glass is a hazard in the yard.
Keep the grades apart. A bag of cans, a stack of frames and a box of castings each get their own price. Tipped in together, the whole lot is paid at the price of the lowest grade.

Take eligible cans to CDS Vic. Victoria's container deposit scheme pays a 10c refund on each eligible drink can, which is far more than it's worth as scrap. We'll take the cans that aren't eligible along with the rest of your aluminium.
Drain the oil from any engine parts, then bring it all to our Hallam yard. We'll grade it, weigh it and pay you by bank transfer the same day.

title: What We Can't Take, and Where It Can Go Instead
description: Gas bottles, lithium batteries, gassed-up fridges, fuel drums and asbestos can't come to the yard. Here's why, and where to take them instead.

body.text: We buy almost anything made of metal, but a few things can't come over our scales, even when they're mostly metal. They're dangerous to handle, crush or cut, and some are against the law to scrap. Here's what to leave at home, and what to do with it instead.

Gas bottles and LPG tanks. We can't take them at the yard, in our bins or with a pickup, even when they're empty. If summer has left you with an old barbecue bottle, your gas supplier or local council can tell you where to drop it off.
Aerosol cans. Even an empty can can hold some propellant, which can catch fire when it's crushed. Your council can tell you how to get rid of them.

Lithium batteries. Phone, laptop, power tool, e-bike and e-scooter batteries can start fires when they're damaged, so they can't go anywhere near scrap metal. Take them to a B-cycle drop-off point instead; many supermarkets and hardware stores have one.

Fridges and air conditioners that still hold gas. Releasing refrigerant gas is illegal, so we can only take them once a licensed technician has removed it. Washing machines, dryers, dishwashers, stoves and ovens are fine as they are.

Drums and tanks with fuel, oil or chemicals in them. Drain tanks, gearboxes and machinery before they come in. Oil, fuel and coolant are hazardous waste, and your council can tell you where to take them.

Asbestos, and anything contaminated with it. Asbestos wasn't banned in Australia until the end of 2003, so older sheds, cladding and fencing can still contain it. We can't take metal that's mixed with it or covered in its dust. Leave it where it is and get advice from a licensed asbestos removalist.
Not sure about something? Send us a photo before you load it up, and we'll let you know whether we can take it.

title: Why We Ask for Photo ID and Pay by Bank Transfer
description: Victorian law means every scrap seller shows photo ID and is paid by bank transfer, not cash. What to bring, and why.

body.text: Some people are surprised that selling a bucket of scrap means showing photo ID and giving us a BSB, and that we don't hand over cash. It isn't our choice: it's how scrap metal is bought and sold in Victoria, and every scrap metal dealer in the state has to work the same way.

We record who we buy from. Victorian law requires us to record the ID of everyone who sells us scrap metal. A driver licence is the easiest. If you don't have one, ask us what else we can accept before you come in.
No cash, by law. Scrap metal dealers in Victoria can't pay in cash, so we pay by bank transfer, the same day your metal is weighed. Bring your BSB and account number along with your scrap.

Why the rules exist. Metal theft hurts everyone: copper pipe taken from building sites, catalytic converters cut from parked cars, cable pulled out of the ground. Recording sellers and paying into a bank account makes stolen metal much harder to sell, which protects honest sellers as well as the people being stolen from.
Businesses get a record too. Every commercial load is weighed and comes with a weigh ticket showing the metal and its weight, so you can track what you've sold.
Come prepared and the paperwork is quick. Bring your photo ID and bank details, and if you're not sure what you need, call us before you come.

title: Copper Grades Explained: Why Clean Copper Pays More
description: Bare bright wire, clean pipe and dirty copper are each paid differently. How copper is graded, and the few minutes of work that lift the price.

body.text: Copper pays more per kilo than any other common scrap metal, but not all copper is paid the same. It's graded on how clean it is, and the gap between the top grade and the bottom can be a big part of what your load is worth.
Bare bright wire is the top grade. That's bare, uncoated copper wire with no solder, paint or tarnish, such as stripped heavy cable, busbar and earth strap.
Clean pipe comes next. That's copper pipe and offcuts with the fittings, solder and insulation removed. Plumbing and air-con offcuts usually land here once they're cleaned up.

Then the lower grades. Painted, soldered, tinned or tarnished copper drops a grade, and pipe with brass fittings or steel brackets still on drops further. We buy copper wire stripped, not with the insulation on.

A few minutes with a hacksaw pays. Cut off brass fittings and steel brackets, pull off foam lagging and tape, and keep bare wire apart from pipe. The brass you cut off is worth money too, so keep it in its own bucket rather than throwing it out.
Never burn wire to get the copper out. It's illegal in Victoria, the smoke is toxic, and burnt copper is graded lower than clean stripped wire.
Old copper hot water cylinders are welcome. Drain them, take off the outer case if there is one, and cut off the fittings if you can.

Ask us what held your load back. If your copper was paid at a lower grade, we'll show you why, so you know for next time. Plumbers, electricians and air-con installers with regular offcuts can ask us about a bin on site.

title: Clearing Old Machinery Off the Farm
description: Old tractors, implements and trailers are worth their weight in steel. How to get farm machinery ready for a pickup and paid for by bank transfer the same day.

body.text: Most farms have a corner where old machinery goes to retire: a tractor that hasn't started in years, a plough, a slasher, a rusted-out trailer, a pile of old fencing. It's all worth money as scrap, and we can come and collect it.

Decide what's scrap. We pay scrap prices, by weight. If a machine still runs and is worth something second-hand, you'll usually get more by selling it as it is. Anything past that point is worth its weight in steel and cast iron.

Take off the valuable parts if you have time. Electric motors, brass fittings and aluminium parts are worth more than steel, and taken off, they're paid at their own price. Take out any batteries and gas bottles too: we don't buy batteries, and gas bottles have to stay behind.
Drain the fluids. Oil, fuel and hydraulic fluid should come out before the pickup. If you can't drain something, tell us when you book, so we can plan for it.
Clear the way. Make sure our truck can get close, and pull rubbish, timber and tyres away from the pile. Let us know if anything is bolted down or hard to reach.

Send us photos. Tell us what's there, roughly how big it is and how to get to it, and we'll give you a price for the metal, let you know about any collection charge and book a pickup that suits. We can take most machinery whole, so there's usually no need to cut anything up.
We collect from farms and rural properties across Melbourne's south-east. Everything is weighed at our Hallam yard, and you're paid by bank transfer the same day.

title: Scrap Metal for Businesses: Sorting, Bins and Weigh Tickets
description: How workshops, builders and manufacturers get more for their scrap: separate bins for valuable metals, regular swaps and a weigh ticket for every load.

body.text: If your business turns out offcuts, swarf, old stock or worn-out equipment, that metal has value. Most workshops and builders already sell their scrap, and the ones who get the most for it keep the metals apart on site.

Separate the valuable metals. Copper, brass, aluminium and stainless steel are each worth far more than steel, but mixed into a steel bin they're paid at the steel price. A small bin or drum for each one, close to where the offcuts are made, earns more than one big mixed bin.

Size the bins to your output. We have bins in different sizes, but most businesses end up with 1 m³ or 2.4 m³ bins. A one-person workshop might keep one bin and call us when it's full. A busy fabrication shop might want a swap on a set day each week. Tell us which metals you produce and how fast, and we'll set it up.
Keep swarf dry and drained. Turnings and shavings from machining are bought too, as long as they're drained of oil and kept apart by metal, as brass swarf with steel in it is paid at a lower rate.

Keep the weigh tickets. Every load is weighed at our Hallam yard and comes with a weigh ticket showing the metal and its weight. With the end of the financial year coming up, those tickets are a simple record of what you've sold and recycled. Your accountant can tell you how to treat the income.
Every load is paid by bank transfer the same day it's weighed. Scrap metal dealers in Victoria can't pay in cash.

We work with fabricators and engineering shops, builders and demolition crews, plumbers, electricians and air-con installers, mechanics and panel shops, manufacturers and farms. If you're not sure your metal is worth collecting, ask us.

title: Is It Stainless Steel? The Magnet Test and Other Clues
description: Stainless steel pays far more than ordinary steel. Use a magnet and its weight to spot it, learn the common grades, and strip it for the best price.

body.text: Stainless steel pays far more than ordinary steel, thanks to the nickel and chromium in it, so it's worth spotting before it ends up in the steel pile. Here's how to tell what you've got.

Try a magnet. On the common 304 and 316 grades, a magnet barely sticks, if at all. If it grabs hard, you've got magnetic stainless or plated steel. Magnetic stainless is still bought, but at a lower rate.
Check the weight. Stainless is heavy for its size. Aluminium can look similar and a magnet won't stick to it either, but it's about a third of the weight.

Know where it turns up. Kitchen sinks, laundry tubs, splashbacks, benches and shelving are usually 304. Marine fittings and dairy, chemical and food-processing equipment are often 316, which pays more. Magnetic 400-series stainless turns up in some appliances, cutlery and exhausts.

Strip off what isn't stainless. Tanks and benches with steel frames, legs, motors, plastic or rubber still attached are paid at a lower rate until they're stripped, so unbolting the legs from an old bench is usually worth the effort.
Keep magnetic stainless separate. We check every piece with a magnet at the yard, so you're paid for what you actually have, but sorting it yourself makes your visit quicker.

Pulling out a commercial kitchen or a café fit-out? We'll take the benches, sinks, shelving and equipment, and for a big job we can collect. Smaller loads can come to our Hallam yard, where we'll weigh them and pay you by bank transfer the same day.

title: Ferrous or Non-Ferrous? Why It Matters When You Sell Scrap
description: Every load of scrap that comes over our scales is sorted into two big families: ferrous and non-ferrous. Knowing which is which is the quickest way to understand what your scrap is worth.

body.text: Every load of scrap that comes over our scales is sorted into two big families: ferrous and non-ferrous. Knowing which is which is the quickest way to understand what your scrap is worth.

Ferrous metals contain iron. Steel and cast iron are the common ones: roofing, fencing, machinery frames, old tools and white goods. There's a lot of it about and it's heavy, so it's paid by the tonne, at a lower rate per kilo than non-ferrous metal.

Non-ferrous metals don't contain iron. Copper, brass, aluminium and stainless steel are the ones we see most. They're worth more per kilo, sometimes many times more, so even a small bucket of copper offcuts or brass fittings can be worth the trip.

The easiest test is a magnet. If it sticks firmly, the metal is ferrous. If it doesn't stick, it's probably non-ferrous and worth keeping apart. Stainless steel is the exception that catches people out: most grades are only slightly magnetic or not magnetic at all, but it's still graded on its own.

Keep the two apart as you collect. A mixed load is paid at the rate of its cheapest metal, but sorted bins of copper, brass, aluminium and steel are each paid at their own price. Not sure what something is? Bring it in and we'll grade it for you.

title: How to Prepare Your Scrap Metal for the Yard
description: A little preparation before you load the ute makes your visit quicker and puts more money in your account. Here's what we suggest.

body.text: A little preparation before you load the ute makes your visit quicker and puts more money in your account. Here's what we suggest.

Sort by metal. Keep copper, brass, aluminium and stainless steel apart from steel and from each other. Each is weighed and paid on its own, so sorting at home means nothing gets paid at a lower grade than it should.

Take off what isn't metal. Plastic, rubber, timber and concrete add weight but aren't paid for, and heavily contaminated metal is graded lower. Unscrewing a plastic handle or knocking off a timber base is usually worth the few minutes.

Strip copper wire. We buy copper wire stripped, not with the insulation on. Clean, bare copper is also worth more than copper still attached to brass fittings. Thin cable takes a long time to strip for very little copper, so it's often not worth the effort.
Drain anything that held fluids. Motors, gearboxes and machinery should be drained of oil and fuel. Leave gas bottles and LPG tanks at home, though: we can't take them, even empty.

Bring your photo ID and bank details. Victorian law requires us to record the ID of everyone who sells us scrap metal, and we pay the same day by bank transfer rather than cash, so have your BSB and account number handy.
